#oat.csv
library(readr)
oat <- read_csv("oat.csv")
Rows: 20 Columns: 2

dbl (2): grain, yield

View(oat)

#1) During an oat harvest, the number of grains in each ear of oat harvested 
#affects the total yield of cereals.

#2) There are two variables, grain and yield, and both are composed of numerical 
#data. For both, the numerical data is composed of continuous data.

#3) The response variable (dependent variable) is the yield. The focal predictor
#(independent variable) is grain. I don't believe there are any covarieties in 
#this dataset.

#4) To print the tables directly into the console, I entered the name of the 
#dataset:

oat
# A tibble: 20 × 2
    grain yield
    <dbl> <dbl>

#Column "grain" displays all 20 data recorded under grain. Column "yield"
#displays all 20 data recorded under yield.

#5)
#Dot Charts:
dotchart(oat$grain, xlab = "Grain")
dotchart(oat$yield, xlab = "Yield")

#Boxplots:
boxplot(oat$grain, xlab = "Grain")
boxplot(oat$yield, xlab = "Yield")

#Histograms:
hist(oat$grain, xlab = "Grain")
hist(oat$yield, xlab = "Yield")

#6)
#Scatterplot:
plot(oat$grain,oat$yield, xlab = "Grain", ylab = "Yield")

#Almost all of the data plots in a nearly perfect vertical line. That is because
#most of the grain values fall within the range of 17.76-28.94, well below 500.
#However, there is a single outlier, plotted to the far right of the graph. This
#point represents a value of 2,528.00, the outlier in the data collected
#under "grain". This single outlier unbalances the data.

#bacteria.csv
library(readr)
bacteria <- read_csv("bacteria.csv")
Rows: 80 Columns: 3                                                                       
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): species, diagnosis
dbl (1): toxin

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
View(bacteria)

#1) The appearance of carcinoma, the most common type of cancer, may be related
#to specific pathogenic bacteria discovered within the bodies of inflicted
#patients.

#2) There are three variables, species, diagnosis, and toxin, in this dataset.
#The variables species and diagnosis, are both categorical data. However,
#the variable species is ordinal because it has an alphabetical ordered ranking,
#while the variable diagnosis is nominal because it has no mathematical or 
#alphabetical ranking. The variable toxin is composed of continuous numerical 
#data.

#3) The response variable (dependent variable) is the toxin. The focal 
#predictor (independent variable) is the species. The diagnosis appears to be
#independent of the species and toxin, so it is an independent variable that
#is not being directly tested, but may have an impact on the collected data,
#making it a covariety.

#4) To print the tables directly into the console, I entered the name of the 
#dataset:

bacteria
# A tibble: 80 × 3
   species diagnosis      toxin
   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
 1 bacterA carc.intestine  1.74
 2 bacterA carc.intestine  2.08
 3 bacterA carc.intestine  1.65
 4 bacterA carc.intestine  1.91
 5 bacterA carc.intestine  2.16
 6 bacterB carc.intestine  1.32
 7 bacterB carc.intestine  1.44
 8 bacterB carc.intestine  1.49
 9 bacterB carc.intestine  1.43
10 bacterB carc.intestine  1.29
# ℹ 70 more rows
# ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

#Since there are a lot of rows in this dataset, I will not print the entirety of
#it here. You can see that column "species" lists the species of bacteria,
#"diagnosis" lists the diagnoses, and "toxin" lists the numeric levels of toxin
#found within the patients' bodies.

#5)
#Dot Chart:
dotchart(bacteria$toxin, xlab = "Toxin")

#Boxplot:
boxplot(bacteria$toxin, xlab = "Toxin")

#Histogram:
hist(bacteria$toxin, xlab = "Toxin")

#6)
#Scatterplot:
interaction.plot(x.factor = bacteria$species,trace.factor = bacteria$diagnosis,response = bacteria$toxin, type = "p", col = 1:4, pch = 1:4, xlab = "Species", ylab = "Toxin Amount", trace.label = "Diagnosis", legend = F)
legend("top", title = "Diagnosis", leg.txt <- c("appendicitis","carc.intestine","carc.rectum","skin.abscess"), col=1:4, pch=1:4)

#Plotting the mean of the toxin amount in relation to the bacteria species and 
#diagnosis reveals a potential association. Diagnosis of appendicitis and skin
#abscesses are often much lower in toxin amount across bacteria species than 
#their carc.intestine and car.rectum counterparts. This difference in toxin 
#amount is apparently clear in bacteria A and bacteria D. Overall, I would say 
#the data is balanced, with general trends -- carc.intestine and car.rectum 
#having greater toxin amounts; appendicitis and skin abscess having lower toxin 
#amounts -- seen across the graph.
